strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: explaining predictions through interpretable concepts when omitted concepts can create confounding. This has a clear audience in causal discovery, explainability, and model auditing.

Using FCI and PAGs with the background constraint that predictions cannot cause image features is principled under the stated causal assumptions. Representing uncertainty about causal ancestry is a valuable aspect of the proposal.

The synthetic example and two annotated image applications make the workflow concrete. The writing clearly explains the distinction between population-level and individual explanations and discusses limitations involving background knowledge and feature selection.
weaknesses: Necessary: Correct the interpretation of the empirical graphs in Sections 6.3–6.4 and Figures 8–10. Pooling directed and partially directed edges measures stability of a cause-or-possible-cause classification; it does not establish causal importance. Likewise, absence of adjacency to the prediction does not exclude an indirect causal effect. Figure 10 itself permits Cardiomegaly to affect the prediction through Atelectasis despite its zero adjacency stability in Figure 8. Report definite and possible ancestry separately and qualify claims that other features are causally irrelevant.

Necessary: Address selection bias in the X-ray experiment. Selecting pneumonia cases and controls with 'no findings' makes inclusion depend on disease and explanatory findings. This can introduce selection-induced dependencies, whereas Section 3 explicitly sets selection bias aside. The manuscript must justify the causal interpretation under this sampling scheme, account for selection, or narrow the clinical conclusions.

Necessary: Repair or remove the Shapley counterexample in Section 3.3 and Appendix A. Appendix A.2 retains the supposedly unobserved Z3 at a fixed value instead of deriving an estimator from the observed variables. Moreover, under the stated SCM, interventions on Z2 or Z3 change Z1, which several 'valid' coalition expectations in A.1 do not reflect. Precisely define the coalition intervention and observable estimator before concluding that omitted confounding produces the advertised attribution failure.

Necessary: Provide stronger support for the reliability of the conditional-independence tests, or present the real-data findings as exploratory hypotheses. Chi-square tests with 26 multilevel bird attributes and conditioning sets of up to four variables raise substantial sparse-cell concerns; the X-ray analysis has only 240 images with potentially rare findings. No cell-count diagnostics or test-calibration assessment is provided, and bootstrapping does not resolve systematic testing errors. Clarify which data split supplies the graph-learning observations and assess whether the reported orientations withstand appropriate testing choices.

Optional: A comparison using the same concept annotations would better isolate the contribution of causal discovery. The selected LIME and SHAP visualizations mainly demonstrate differences in explanatory representation and scope. Controlled interventions in the synthetic images would also strengthen validation of the learned causal exclusions.
